objective: Build a barcode-scanning damaged stock write-off system for warehouse operations that captures item details, damage photos, and values, routes them to supervisors for approval, and includes a practical damage severity assessment from uploaded photos. The system must handle ~400 write-offs monthly, maintain staff-only data privacy, and provide reporting on write-off history and trends without integrations to external systems, while accommodating real warehouse conditions including poor lighting and intermittent connectivity.
architecture:
Warehouse staff use a native mobile app (React Native) to scan item barcodes using the device camera with platform-optimized scanning libraries (iOS AVFoundation, Android ML Kit Barcode Scanning). The app sends the barcode to the serverless backend (AWS Lambda via API Gateway), which validates the barcode against the internal inventory database (Aurora Serverless PostgreSQL) and returns the matching item details (SKU, description, current stock count). Staff then complete a damage report form: they select a damage reason from a pre-defined dropdown, upload a photo (captured via device camera), and enter a mandatory value (no auto-fill from stale data). The app stores submissions locally in an offline queue when connectivity is poor, then syncs when reconnected.

The backend Lambda stores the pending write-off in Aurora with a status of 'Pending', includes the photo in AWS S3, and triggers a practical damage assessment. Instead of an unsuitable classification model, a heuristic analysis runs: the Lambda calculates the percentage of dark/defect pixels in the uploaded photo (using sharp library for image analysis) and combines this with the selected damage reason to produce a severity tier (Low/Medium/High). This tier is stored with the write-off record.

Supervisors access a responsive web dashboard (React web app) that lists pending write-offs with key details and the severity tier. They can review each write-off, view the photo, see the severity assessment, and either approve or reject with a mandatory comment for rejections. Approval changes the write-off status to 'Approved', triggers an inventory deduction for that SKU in the internal stock table, and logs the final value. Rejection sets status to 'Rejected' with the comment stored.

Reporting dashboards (built with Chart.js) allow both mobile app and web users to view historical write-offs filtered by date range, SKU, damage reason, or severity tier, showing aggregate values and trends. All data remains within the system; no integrations with external inventory or accounting systems occur. The serverless architecture scales to zero during off-hours, and the mobile app provides offline submission capability.

tech_stack.rationale: React Native provides true native barcode scanning via platform-specific APIs (AVFoundation on iOS, ML Kit on Android) that work reliably in warehouse lighting conditions with auto-focus and distance handling; Expo simplifies development and deployment. The leading alternative, a PWA with QuaggaJS, was rejected because browser-based scanning fails in real warehouse conditions with poor lighting and varying distances. The main limitation is requiring app store deployment, but this ensures reliable scanning essential for warehouse operations.

Lambda provides serverless compute that scales to zero during off-hours (warehouse closed nights/weekends), matching the intermittent usage pattern (~400 write-offs/month) while minimizing costs. The leading alternative, EC2 24/7, was rejected because it creates unnecessary operational overhead and cost for a system with predictable idle periods. The main limitation is Lambda cold starts could add latency, but write-off submissions are not ultra-time-sensitive and provisioned concurrency can mitigate.

Aurora Serverless automatically scales capacity up and down based on workload, with ability to pause during periods of inactivity, perfectly matching warehouse operating hours and minimizing cost. The leading alternative, RDS fixed instance, was rejected because 24/7 operation for intermittent usage is cost-inefficient. The main limitation is that scaling operations have brief latency, but write-off workflows tolerate seconds of delay.

tech_stack.choice: AWS API Gateway + Lambda + Aurora Serverless + S3
tech_stack.rationale: AWS serverless stack eliminates the need for always-on EC2 instances; API Gateway routes requests to Lambda functions; Aurora Serverless handles database; S3 stores photos with lifecycle policies. The leading alternative, Google Cloud Run with Cloud SQL, was rejected because AWS's serverless database (Aurora Serverless) provides better cost optimization for intermittent usage than Cloud SQL's fixed instances. The main limitation is that Aurora Serverless v1 has minimum ACU capacity when active, but still cheaper than 24/7 RDS.

tech_stack.choice: Heuristic image analysis with sharp library
tech_stack.rationale: A practical heuristic approach analyzes uploaded photos for defect pixel percentage (dark/abnormal areas) and combines with damage reason to produce a severity tier (Low/Medium/High) that correlates better with warehouse judgment than arbitrary classification scores. The leading alternative, Google Vertex AI Vision with CLIP model, was rejected because it produces meaningless severity scores for damage assessment, being trained for object classification not damage regression. The main limitation is that the heuristic may miss subtle damage types, but it provides useful guidance without misleading scores.

tech_stack.choice: Platform-native APIs via React Native libraries
tech_stack.rationale: iOS AVFoundation Camera with barcode detection and Android ML Kit Barcode Scanning provide industrial-grade scanning with auto-focus, multiple format support, and reliability in varied lighting/distance conditions. The leading alternative, browser-based QuaggaJS, was rejected because it fails under real warehouse conditions with poor lighting and glare. The main limitation is requiring separate mobile app builds, but this delivers reliable scanning essential for warehouse productivity.

tech_stack.choice: Session cookies with HttpOnly flag and short expiration
tech_stack.rationale: Session cookies stored with HttpOnly flag prevent XSS token theft in shared warehouse device scenarios; short expiration (1-2 hours) and SameSite=Strict provide security for shift-sharing devices. The leading alternative, JWT in localStorage, was rejected because it exposes tokens to XSS attacks on shared warehouse devices left unattended. The main limitation is that mobile app requires different auth pattern (secure storage), but session cookies work well for web supervisor dashboard.

tech_stack.choice: Chart.js embedded in React web dashboard
tech_stack.rationale: Chart.js is a lightweight JavaScript charting library that can render bar charts, line trends, and pie charts for write-off history directly in the React frontend without a separate BI tool. The leading alternative, a dedicated BI tool like Metabase, was rejected because the requirement is for simple reporting within the system and out-of-scope integrations. The main limitation is that Chart.js may become slow if rendering thousands of data points for long date ranges, requiring backend aggregation.

user_flow: Staff opens native mobile app on company device and logs in with employee ID and password (stored securely in device keychain).
Staff points device camera at item barcode; native scanning auto-detects and decodes barcode even in suboptimal lighting/distance.
App fetches item details (SKU, description, current stock) via API (or shows cached data if offline).
Staff selects damage reason from dropdown: 'Water Damage', 'Crushed', 'Torn Packaging', 'Expired', 'Other'.
Staff captures photo of damaged item using device camera (app ensures adequate lighting guidance).
App shows preview of uploaded photo.
Staff enters mandatory write-off value (no auto-fill from potentially stale data).
Staff taps 'Submit for Approval' - if offline, submission queues locally and syncs when connectivity resumes.
App confirms submission and shows pending ID.
Supervisor logs in via web browser on desktop or tablet using session cookie authentication.
Supervisor sees list with columns: SKU, description, damage reason, severity tier (Low/Medium/High), submitted by, date.
Supervisor clicks a row to view details: full item info, photo, severity tier with reasoning, submitted value.
Supervisor either: Approves with optional comment, or Rejects with mandatory comment.
If approved, system deducts stock count for that SKU in inventory and marks write-off as approved.
If rejected, system marks write-off as rejected with comment visible to original staff.
Staff can later view status of their submissions in mobile app under 'My Submissions'.

Both staff (mobile app) and supervisor (web) can navigate to 'Reports', select date range, filter by SKU/damage reason/severity tier, and view charts of total write-offs, aggregate value, and trends over time.

page_behavior.description: Simple form with employee ID and password fields; submits to backend for session cookie creation with HttpOnly flag. Invalid credentials show error. On success, redirects based on role: supervisor to /pending.
Native login screen storing credentials securely in device keychain; authentication tokens managed via secure storage.
Native camera view with barcode scanning overlay, using platform-optimized scanning that works in varied lighting. Includes manual entry fallback with SKU validation.

Form with: read-only item details (SKU, description, current stock), dropdown for damage reason (required), camera integration for photo capture, value field (mandatory, no auto-fill), submit button. Includes offline queue indicator.

Table listing pending write-offs with columns: SKU, description, damage reason, severity tier (colored: Low green, Medium yellow, High red), submitted by, date. Each row clickable to open detail modal.

Modal showing: item details, photo (full view), severity tier with defect percentage and damage reason context, submitted value, and two buttons: 'Approve' (opens comment optional field) and 'Reject' (requires comment). Action triggers status update and inventory deduction if approved.
Staff view of their own write-offs with status (Pending/Approved/Rejected) and review comment if rejected. Shows sync status for offline submissions.

Dashboard with date range picker, filters for SKU, damage reason, severity tier. Charts: bar chart of write-off count by reason, line chart of daily aggregate value, pie chart of severity distribution. Data fetched via API /api/writeoffs/reports.
Simplified reporting view showing personal submission trends and aggregate warehouse data when connected.

security_design: Authentication: Employee ID and password hashed with bcrypt; web sessions use HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict and 2-hour expiration for shared device security.
Mobile app authentication: Secure credential storage in device keychain, tokens with 4-hour expiration requiring re-auth.
Authorization: Frontend routes guard based on role (staff cannot access web /pending). Backend endpoints enforce role checks via middleware.
Data isolation: Staff can only see their own submissions; supervisors see all. API ensures employee_id matches ownership or role.
Photo storage: S3 bucket private; signed URLs generated with 5-minute expiry for frontend photo viewing; no public access.
Input validation: Barcode input validated against SKU regex; damage reason from allowed enum; photo file type restricted to JPEG, PNG; file size limit 5MB.
SQL injection prevention: Parameterized queries via pg library; no raw SQL concatenation.
HTTPS enforcement: All traffic over TLS; backend sets HSTS headers.
Sensitive data: No customer or payment data stored as per requirement; employee names and IDs are internal only.
Session management: Web sessions automatically expire after 2 hours of inactivity; mobile app requires biometric re-auth after 4 hours.
Audit trail: Inventory transactions log every stock deduction with timestamp and writeoff_id; write-off review_comment stored for rejections.
Shared device protection: Web sessions clear on browser close; recommend dedicated devices per user where possible.
deployment_and_operations: CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipeline for backend Lambda functions and web dashboard; Expo build pipeline for mobile app distribution via app stores.
Database migrations: Use node-pg-migrate for schema changes; migrations run via Lambda on deployment.
Monitoring: AWS CloudWatch for Lambda invocations, error rates, Aurora Serverless capacity units; Xray for tracing API calls.
Backup: Aurora Serverless automated backups retained for 30 days; S3 versioning enabled for photos with lifecycle policy to transition to Glacier after 90 days.
Rollback: Lambda function versions allow quick rollback; Aurora Serverless maintains point-in-time recovery.
Scaling: Aurora Serverless automatically scales between 2-8 ACUs based on workload; Lambda scales automatically with concurrency limits.
Cost optimization: Aurora Serverless can pause during predictable off-hours (nights, weekends) via scheduler; Lambda cold starts managed with provisioned concurrency during warehouse hours.
Health checks: API Gateway health check on /health endpoint returning 200 if Lambda can connect to Aurora.
Failure handling: Mobile app offline queue ensures submissions aren't lost during connectivity issues; sync retries with exponential backoff.
Safe state: Aurora transactions ensure inventory deductions only on approved write-offs; pending write-offs remain pending until supervisor action.

timeline.phase: Phase 1: Serverless Foundation & Mobile App Core
timeline.description: Set up AWS serverless infrastructure (API Gateway, Lambda, Aurora Serverless, S3), create Item and User tables, implement authentication for both web (session cookies) and mobile (secure storage). Build React Native app skeleton with login and navigation.

timeline.description: Integrate native barcode scanning libraries (iOS AVFoundation, Android ML Kit) into mobile app, implement scan screen and damage form with offline queue, backend API for barcode validation and pending write-off storage, S3 photo upload flow.

timeline.phase: Phase 3: Heuristic Severity Assessment & Supervisor Web
timeline.description: Implement heuristic image analysis (defect pixel percentage calculation using sharp library), combine with damage reason to produce severity tiers, build responsive web dashboard for supervisors with /pending table and detail modal.
Implement approval/reject endpoints with inventory deduction logic, create InventoryTransaction table, add offline sync mechanism for mobile app, implement web session management.
Develop /reports page with Chart.js for web, implement filters and aggregations, add mobile app reports view, conduct user testing with warehouse staff in actual lighting conditions.
App store submission for mobile app, final security review, configure Aurora Serverless scheduling for cost optimization, deploy to production, create user documentation, train supervisors and staff.

assumptions: Warehouse staff have company-provided mobile devices (iOS/Android) capable of running the native app with camera access.
Barcodes are standard UPC/EAN or internal SKU codes compatible with native platform scanners.
Item inventory (SKU, description) is pre-loaded into the system via separate admin interface; values are entered manually per write-off.
Supervisors have desktop or tablet devices for web dashboard access.
Internet connectivity is available in most warehouse areas but may have dead zones; offline submission capability handles intermittent connectivity.
Photo file sizes are reasonable (<5MB) per upload; warehouse lighting varies but native camera handles better than browser camera.
Severity tier (Low/Medium/High) is advisory; supervisor makes final approval decision regardless of assessment.
No integration with external accounting systems; write-off value is recorded internally only from manual entry.
Employee IDs are unique and known; user provisioning is manual or via separate process.
Company accepts app store distribution for the mobile app rather than requiring browser-only access.
open_questions: Should the heuristic severity assessment be visible to staff during submission or only to supervisors? The analysis occurs server-side after upload.
What is the exact list of damage reasons and their mapping to severity tiers? Need final enum values from warehouse management.
Is there a requirement for bulk approval (e.g., approve all pending for a given SKU) or must each write-off be individually reviewed?
What retention policy for photos and write-off records? S3 lifecycle policy currently archives to Glacier after 90 days.
Should the system enforce a maximum write-off value threshold requiring higher-level approval? Not specified.
How should barcode scanning handle items with multiple barcodes (e.g., case pack vs unit)? Native scanners detect all formats.
Will the company approve app store distribution costs and review processes for the mobile app?
What is the exact formula for defect pixel percentage analysis? Need to calibrate thresholds for Low/Medium/High tiers based on sample damage photos.
How to handle items without barcodes? Manual SKU entry with validation needed.
Should there be a separate 'Admin' role for managing users and inventory items beyond the scope?

Unresolved design review finding (high, tech_stack): The AI vision model requirement ('AI grading of damage severity from uploaded photos') is being replaced with a heuristic pixel analysis that will fail on most real damage assessment tasks. Damage severity cannot be assessed by counting 'dark/defect pixels' - this approach fails for: 1) water damage (often subtle discoloration, not dark pixels), 2) crushed packaging (deformation doesn't create dark pixels), 3) torn packaging (tears may appear as regular edges), 4) expired goods (no visual change). The heuristic produces meaningless tiers that supervisors will ignore or distrust, making the feature worthless. Suggested fix: Either remove the AI grading requirement from scope, or implement a proper vision model trained on actual damaged goods images. Use a lightweight model like MobileNetV2 with custom training on warehouse damage images, deployed as a Lambda container.

Unresolved design review finding (high, security_design): Shared warehouse device scenario fails with session cookies approach. In real warehouse operations: 1) Multiple staff share the same device throughout shifts, 2) Sessions don't expire during active shift work, 3) HttpOnly cookies don't prevent one staff member accessing another's submissions after browser restart. This violates data isolation requirement (staff should only see their own submissions). Suggested fix: Implement per-user authentication with explicit logout on shared devices. Use short-lived JWTs (15-30 minutes) with refresh tokens stored server-side, requiring re-authentication after token expiry.

Unresolved design review finding (medium, data_model): The 'value_source' field claims capabilities the chosen components cannot produce. The field suggests future integration with accounting systems ('calculated' option), but the system explicitly states no external integrations. This creates misleading data model expectations and requires handling null/empty values for 'value_source' in all records. Suggested fix: Remove 'value_source' field entirely or limit to single value 'manual' as per current scope. Add comment field if future integration anticipated.

Unresolved design review finding (medium, architecture): Offline queue synchronization fails under real warehouse connectivity patterns. Warehouse dead zones may last hours; mobile app will accumulate submissions that need to sync when connectivity resumes. The design lacks: 1) Conflict resolution when same item is written off multiple times while offline, 2) Handling of stock count updates that occurred while device was offline, 3) Transaction rollback if server rejects submission after local queue acceptance. Suggested fix: Implement optimistic conflict detection with ETag pattern: store current_stock version with offline submission, validate on sync. Add batch synchronization with atomic transaction support.

Unresolved design review finding (medium, user_flow): Mandatory value entry without any guidance will lead to inconsistent valuation in real usage. Warehouse staff without product pricing knowledge will guess values, creating unreliable financial reporting. The rejection of 'stale data' auto-fill means each write-off requires manual research or arbitrary guessing. Suggested fix: Provide reference pricing data (last known value with 'stale' flag) as guidance, or implement simple pricing table lookup based on SKU with manual override capability.

Unresolved design review finding (medium, deployment_and_operations): Aurora Serverless pausing during nights/weekends creates critical failure point for 24/7 warehouse operations. Many warehouses operate night shifts or weekend receiving. Scheduled pausing will cause: 1) Night shift cannot submit write-offs, 2) Weekend operations halt, 3) Cold starts after pause cause unacceptable latency for time-sensitive operations. Suggested fix: Remove Aurora Serverless pausing or implement warm-up Lambda before scheduled shift starts. Consider Aurora Serverless v2 which doesn't pause but scales to minimum capacity.
